context: Each move climbs 1 or 2 stairs. Landing on stair i incurs a nonnegative cost cost[i]. Starting on the ground is free. Let dp[i] be the minimum total cost to reach stair i.
description: Green boxes from dp[1] through dp[9] run left to right. Costs for odd-numbered stairs appear above and those for even-numbered stairs below, with arrows pointing to the corresponding dp boxes. Cost arrows lead directly to dp[1] and dp[2]. Starting at dp[3], a bracket labeled min links the two adjacent predecessors to the next state. A plus sign beside the current cost arrow adds the cost of landing here. Below are the initial states and the general transition dp[i] = min(dp[i-1], dp[i-2]) + cost[i]. No numerical costs are given.
The last move to stair i must start at stair i-1 or i-2. Either way we pay cost[i] for the current stair. Compare the cumulative costs dp[i-1] and dp[i-2], take the lower one, and add cost[i].

From the ground we can reach stair 1 or 2 directly, so dp[1] = cost[1]. Since cost[1] is nonnegative, reaching stair 2 via stair 1 cannot be cheaper than going directly. Thus dp[2] = cost[2]. The table lists the relationships for stairs 1 through 9 by state. The ground as the starting point and the explanation that going directly costs no more than going via stair 1 follow from the rules. The diagram has no separate ground node.

summary: For each state, take the smaller of the previous two minimum cumulative costs and add the cost of the current stair, cost[i].
